title: Analyzing Mixing Inhomogeneity in a Microfluidic Device by Microscale Schlieren Technique
protocol: Draw the outline of a T-microchannel using graphic layout software.
Set the dimensions for the two feed channels at 90 µm wide and 2,500 µm long.
Set the dimensions for the confluence channel at 180 µm wide and 3,000 µm long.
Connect each channel to an individual circle with a diameter of 1,100 µm.
Mark ‘clear’ and ‘dark’ areas on the design for exposure and covered regions respectively.
Transfer the pattern onto a chrome-on-glass photomask using a laser pattern generator with a wavelength of 442 nm.
Create a mold through standard lithography process using the photomask, substrate, and photoresist (e.g., SU-8).
Ensure the photoresist layer is 55.2 µm thick for optimal lithography.
Use the mold to fabricate the T-microchannel with PDMS.
Punch through-holes in PDMS aligned to circular patterns using a stainless steel tube of 2 mm outer diameter.
Treat the surfaces of PDMS and a glass slide with oxygen plasma at 60 W for 30 seconds.
Attach the treated PDMS to the glass slide.
Place the bonded PDMS structure on a hot plate at 120 °C for 5 minutes.
Insert Teflon tubes into the punched holes in the PDMS for fluidic connection.

Construct the microscale schlieren system from a Hoffman modulation contrast microscope by removing the slit plate and replacing it with a knife-edge modulator in the rear focal plane of the 5X objective.
Blacken the surface of the knife-edge to reduce reflectivity.
Mount the high-speed camera to the trinocular tube via a C-mount adapter.
Connect the camera to a desktop computer using an Ethernet cable.
Set the gamma correction for the camera to 1.
Turn on the LED light source.
Use an image processing software to obtain the grayscale values of an acquired image.
Remove the knife-edge from the setup.
Adjust the illumination, aperture, and exposure time so that the average grayscale readout is about 10% less than the maximal value for an 8-bit image.
Record the average grayscale readout with the knife-edge completely blocking incident light as the background intensity for a 100% cutoff.
Insert the knife-edge such that the average grayscale readout of the acquired image lies in the middle of the values for 0% and 100% cutoff, setting the degree of cutoff to 50%.
Prepare two transparent fluids with known refractive indices that are completely miscible with each other as constituents.
Evaluate the dependence of refractive index on concentration of the mixture using literature or the Gladstone-Dale equation.
Choose a designated composition below which the refractive index of the solution varies linearly with the concentration.
Use dilute aqueous ethanol with a mass fraction of 0.05 and water as working fluids for the experiment.
Put the T-microchannel on the specimen stage.
Arrange the T-microchannel so that the confluent channel is parallel to the knife-edge.
Prepare two identical syringes: one filled with water and the other with dilute aqueous ethanol.
Calculate the desired flow rate Q using Q = πd²V/4, where d is the inner diameter of the syringe and V is the speed of the plunger.
Fill syringe A with the reference fluid (water).
Fill syringe B with the working fluid (dilute aqueous ethanol).
Fix the Teflon outlet tube to the beaker's wall and ensure its end is below the liquid level in the beaker.
Start the syringe pumps to deliver fluids into the T-microchannel at identical volume flow rates.
Wait until steady flow establishes.
Record twenty frames of fluidic mixing at a frame rate of 30 fps.
Stop the pump loaded with syringe B.
Pump reference fluid (water) through one inlet into the confluence channel at constant rate.
Wait until steady flow condition is reached and no schlieren pattern is observed.
Take the reference image when no optical inhomogeneity is present in the T-microchannel.
Record twenty frames of the reference image at a frame rate of 30 fps.
Repeat steps from establishing steady flow to recording frames for different Reynolds numbers: Re = 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50.
Divide the acquired image I(i, j) by the reference image I0(i, j).
Construct the three-dimensional model for the geometry of the T-microchannel using an image processing software.
Discretize the flow domain into structured grids.
Employ finer mesh in the confluence and central region of the T-microchannel to increase accuracy.
Assign physical properties of fluids and establish boundary conditions to the flow domain.
Determine concentration-dependent diffusion coefficient from the concentration obtained in the last iteration during solving process.
Examine sensitivities of computed results by performing grid study.

For each node (xi, yi) on the xy-plane, employ CFD post-processing tool to take average values of the concentration field across channel depth by trapezoidal rule: w(xi, yj) = {∑k [w(xi, yj, zk) + w(xi, yj, zk+1)]∙(zk+1 - zk)/2}/D.
Use central differencing scheme to compute derivative of concentration with respect to cross-stream direction: (∂w/∂y)i, j = [w(xi, yj+1) - w(xi, yj-1)]/(yj+1 - yj-1).
Extract ratio of grayscale values I/I0 and gradient of mass fraction ∂w/∂y at specified locations such as y = 0 or various given x.
Plot results to determine relationship between I/I0 and ∂w/∂y: I/I0 = C1∂w/∂y + C2 (C1 and C2 are constants).
Perform linear regression to analyze data.
Repeat steps 3.1 to 3.2 for mixing in the target microfluidic device.
Ensure the depth of the target microfluidic device is identical or close to that of the T-microchannel.
If unsteady phenomenon is expected, acquire a video clip in step 3.1.4 instead.
Set the frame rate high enough to resolve the dynamics of the transient flow clearly.
Maintain the exposure time identical to the value used in steps 2.4, 2.5, 3.1.4, and 3.1.7.
Use the relationship obtained in step 3.6 to convert the ratio of grayscale values to the gradient of mass fraction in the target microfluidic device.
